Newborn Care

Passionflower while breastfeeding: benefits, uncertainty and safer support

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Poor sleep, anxiety or low mood after birth can make a calming herbal remedy appealing. Passionflower has been studied in some adults, but that does not establish its safety for a breastfed baby or make it a treatment for postpartum depression. You deserve effective help that takes both your health and feeding choices seriously.

Which passionflower and which preparation?

Passionflower is a climbing plant with distinctive flowers. The medicinal herb commonly discussed is Passiflora incarnata; the genus contains many other species. An ornamental garden plant, passion fruit eaten as food, a tea, a tincture and a concentrated extract are not interchangeable products. Flower colour or a photograph cannot establish identity, purity or a safe dose.

Leaves and other above-ground parts may be used in herbal preparations. Growing the vine in a warm garden or collecting its flowers does not make a homemade medicine suitable for breastfeeding. Do not forage or prepare an unidentified plant, and do not give passionflower remedies to a baby. A food flavouring is also different from repeated medicinal use.

Traditional uses and the limits of the evidence

Small adult studies suggest possible effects on anxiety, including before procedures, and on some aspects of sleep. Findings are limited or mixed; they do not establish a reliable treatment for every sleep problem, equivalence to a prescribed sedative, or benefit in breastfeeding parents. There is no established evidence that passionflower increases milk supply or treats postpartum depression.

Traditional claims extend to headaches, dizziness, depression, social anxiety, Parkinson's disease, seizures and fibromyalgia; digestive symptoms, cough, earache, menstrual or menopausal symptoms; and cholesterol, heart failure, cancer, wound healing or ageing. These claims should not be presented as proven treatments. Laboratory findings or historical use cannot show that a particular preparation helps people safely. It is not a detox treatment and must not replace care for epilepsy, heart disease, cancer or another diagnosed illness. Other traditional claims concern restlessness or irritability, antioxidant effects, muscle spasms, vision, haemorrhoids, heart-attack risk and support of chemotherapy; these are also unproven uses, not reasons to self-treat.

Why breastfeeding safety remains uncertain

Reliable information about passionflower transfer into human milk and effects on breastfed babies is lacking. Unknown exposure is not the same as no exposure, and no reported harm is not proof of safety. NHS guidance advises avoiding herbal remedies during breastfeeding because adequate safety information is missing; discuss an effective, better studied option with a clinician or pharmacist instead of starting a tea or extract yourself.

The baby's age, prematurity, health and other medicines matter. General short-term safety observations in adults cannot supply a breastfeeding dose, a safe waiting interval between taking it and feeding, or reassurance about concentrated or mixed products. If you have already taken some, keep the packaging and seek individual advice about the product, amount and timing. Do not automatically stop breastfeeding, discard milk or stop a necessary prescribed medicine without advice.

Treat the reason you are seeking a remedy

Persistent sadness, anxiety, loss of interest, difficulty bonding or inability to sleep even when there is a chance to rest deserve assessment. Early baby blues often settle within two weeks, but worsening symptoms or difficulty coping need help sooner. Postpartum depression can begin during pregnancy or within the year after birth; it is treatable and is not a personal failure.

Practical help with meals and baby care, protected rest and supportive conversation can help, alongside professional treatment when needed. Talking therapies and, where appropriate, an individually chosen antidepressant are established options; many medicines can be used while breastfeeding. Do not delay care while trying herbs or use alcohol to manage sleep. New hallucinations, unusual fixed beliefs, extreme agitation or rapidly changing mood after birth require immediate urgent assessment for possible postpartum psychosis.

Side effects, interactions and caregiving

Passionflower can cause drowsiness, dizziness, confusion or poor coordination. These effects can interfere with driving and safely caring for a baby. Other sedating medicines, alcohol or anaesthesia may add to sedation; show the complete product and medicine list to a pharmacist or prescriber, including before a planned operation. Tell the surgical team if you have used it within two weeks of a procedure; they should direct any changes to treatment.

Do not assume that it inevitably damages the liver or pancreas, lowers blood pressure or causes a fast heartbeat. LiverTox has not convincingly linked passionflower to liver injury, but good prospective safety studies are lacking, and this does not establish breastfeeding safety. New troublesome symptoms need assessment, especially with heart or liver disease or a mixed supplement. If a medicine or herb makes you sleepy, do not share a bed with your baby; never sleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair. Use a separate clear cot with a firm, flat surface and place the baby on their back.

Product review and a practical next step

Ask for the exact botanical name, plant part, strength, full ingredient list and formulation. Combination sleep products can contain other herbs or medicines, and similarly named preparations can differ. 'Natural', traditional or sold over the counter does not guarantee quality, effectiveness or safety. Supplements are not necessarily assessed before sale in the same way as medicines; regulation varies by country. A topical product is not automatically a safe substitute, especially where a baby could lick treated skin.

Tell the clinician that you are breastfeeding, why you want the product and whether another pregnancy is possible. NCCIH advises against passionflower use during pregnancy because it may stimulate uterine contractions; this is not a claim that every accidental exposure causes harm. Bring any existing exposure for individual review. Agree on a plan for your sleep or mood, follow-up and suitable treatment rather than choosing an unsupported dose or feeding schedule.

When you or your baby need help

Seek prompt medical advice if the baby feeds poorly, is unusually sleepy or sleeps longer than usual between feeds; do not simply attribute this to a herb. Difficulty breathing, blue, grey or unusually pale colour, a seizure, difficulty waking, inability to wake, floppiness or an abnormal lack of response or loss of consciousness need immediate emergency care. An adult with trouble breathing, swelling of the tongue or throat, fainting or loss of consciousness also needs emergency help; use a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector for suspected anaphylaxis and call emergency services. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

Thoughts of suicide or harming the baby need urgent professional help. If there is immediate danger, inability to stay safe, or severe confusion or behaviour that puts anyone at risk, seek emergency care now and involve a trusted adult to help keep the baby safe. Suspected postpartum psychosis needs immediate urgent assessment even without disclosed thoughts of harm. An app or a herbal product cannot assess the safety of waiting.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring the exact passionflower product and all medicine details to a pharmacist or clinician before use; mention breastfeeding, the baby's health and possible pregnancy.

Ask for assessment of sleep, anxiety or low mood and a treatment plan compatible with your needs; do not replace prescribed care or invent a feeding interval.

After exposure, seek individual advice and watch for feeding or wakefulness changes; obtain urgent or emergency help for the warning signs above.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record sleep, mood, symptoms and questions for an appointment. It cannot identify a plant, measure a herb in milk, establish infant safety, diagnose postpartum depression or psychosis, or decide whether urgent care can wait.

When to seek help

Avoid self-treatment with passionflower during breastfeeding and do not give it to a baby. Seek prompt assessment for infant feeding or wakefulness changes. Breathing difficulty, blue, grey or unusually pale colour, difficulty waking, inability to wake, floppiness or an abnormal lack of response, seizures or loss of consciousness need emergency care. Immediate danger to yourself or the baby requires emergency help; suspected postpartum psychosis requires immediate urgent clinical assessment. Do not stop essential medicines or breastfeeding automatically after exposure; get individual advice. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Passionflower has limited adult anxiety and sleep research, not established breastfeeding or postpartum-depression benefits.
  • Avoid self-starting a medicinal tea, extract or mixed product while breastfeeding; ask for a better studied option.
  • After an exposure, obtain individual advice rather than automatically stopping breastfeeding or a prescribed treatment.
  • Sedation can affect caregiving: avoid bed-sharing when drowsy and never sleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair.
  • An unresponsive or breathless baby, immediate risk of harm or serious adult symptoms require emergency help; suspected postpartum psychosis requires immediate urgent assessment.

Frequently asked questions

What are passionflower's traditional benefits?

It has been used for anxiety, sleep and many unrelated symptoms. Small adult studies are limited; traditional or laboratory claims do not establish treatment for neurological, digestive, heart or other diseases.

Does it benefit breastfeeding or postpartum depression?

There is no established benefit for milk supply or postpartum depression. Seek assessment for low mood, anxiety or sleep problems; effective treatments can often be chosen while continuing breastfeeding.

Is passionflower safe while breastfeeding?

Safety and milk-transfer data are insufficient. Do not start a medicinal preparation yourself. A pharmacist or clinician should review the exact product, your health, other medicines and the baby's age and condition.

What side effects matter?

Drowsiness, dizziness, confusion and poor coordination can affect you and caregiving. Infant effects through milk are not adequately known. New symptoms need assessment; absence of a proven liver-injury link does not establish overall safety.

Is tea or a garden flower safer than an extract?

Not reliably. Species, plant parts, concentration and other ingredients differ. A homemade tea has no established breastfeeding dose, and a photograph cannot confirm plant identity. Do not give the remedy to a baby.

Should I stop breastfeeding after taking it once?

Not automatically. Keep the package and contact a pharmacist or clinician with the amount, time and baby's details. Obtain urgent help for poor feeding or unusual sleepiness, and emergency care if the baby is difficult or impossible to wake, is floppy or unresponsive, looks blue, grey or unusually pale, or has breathing difficulty. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

Can I combine it with sleeping medicines or use it before surgery?

Do not add it without a medicine review: sedation may be increased. Tell the surgical team about recent use, including within two weeks of a procedure. Do not stop necessary prescribed treatment on your own.

When is postpartum distress urgent?

Get help promptly for worsening mood or inability to cope, without waiting two weeks. Possible psychosis needs immediate urgent assessment. Immediate danger, suicidal intent, inability to stay safe, severe confusion or risk to the baby require emergency help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
